The Framing Narratives of the “Green Data Center” Project in Mongolia¶

By Khatanbuuvei Battulga

Submitted in partial fulfillment of the requirements for SOSC 314: Computational Social Science

Duke Kunshan University

Professor: Markus Neumann, PhD

Fall 2026

Background¶

UNCCD hosted its 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, last August under the theme Restoring Land, Restoring Hope. Its aim was to find solutions to desertification, land degradation, and drought by bringing together leaders, scientists, youth, indigenous people, pastoralists, and farmers, and facilitating various discussions and meetings among them (UNCCD 17th Session of the Conference of the Parties, n.d.).

One of the main outcomes achieved from the conference in terms of the economy was the agreement to position Mongolia as a new global data center hub, with a capacity of 863 megawatts. This decision was achieved due to Mongolia’s advantages: cheap renewable energy, a naturally cold climate that will reduce cooling costs, vast land, and a stable legal environment (Brkic, 2026). The project will be held under the title “Green Data Center”.

Ever since this news had come out, the public was divided. Some say this brings global attention, investments, and economic circles to Mongolia. Others say it overlooks the detrimental environmental effects data centers result in. Therefore, this study aims to analyze how the news articles across Mongolian media are framing this proposed initiative.

Motivation¶

News sources may selectively emphasise economic development, technological modernization, resource constraints, or environmental risks to write articles hovering around this proposed project. Analyzing these frames reveals how the project is publicly presented and contested. Ideally, official news sources should present factual information with a neutral tone, allowing the public to form their own opinion. However, a selective dominance of a single framing may lead to negligence for other issues that exist but haven’t been equally presented.

A successful implementation of this project would examine how accurately automated methods such as logistic regression identify frames in news articles compared with the frame assignments that a human has closely read and identified. It will also inspect if some frames dominantly appear across the coverage of Mongolia's proposed Green Data Center initiative and explore whether different institutions construct the issue differently across various news sources.

Research Question¶

Are there any dominant opportunity and risk frames in Mongolian online news coverage of the recently proposed Green Data Center initiative, and how does the prevalence of frames differ between official government sources and independent news sources?

Data¶

In the scope of this project, articles reporting on the proposed “Green Data Center” project by Mongolian news websites and government portals will be studied and the unit of analysis will be one article.

An initial sample of 64 articles was collected; however, 50 were retained after checking study-period eligibility (May 13th, 2026 onward), missing text, relevance, and exact duplicates.

The first batch of relevant articles according to their publication date (May 13th) included reports on the intent to introduce the initiative during COP17, setting the start of the study period.

In preprocessing, the trafilatura library on Python was employed to extract the main text from menu, ads, and other irrelevant content. Main text from 8 articles couldn't be downloaded and extracted due to domain resolution issues, block from robots.txt (a website file that decides whether automated programs have access), HTTP 403 message (Forbidden) from the servers, and inability of trafilatura to extract the text. Additionally, eight articles formed four pairs of exact duplicates. One article from each pair was retained, and the other was excluded.

For the remaining articles, their text was normalized using Unicode, a system that assigns a unique code to every character used by computational methods, including the Mongolian letters, such as Ө and Ү, that are not in other Cyrillic alphabets, for normalization. Every word in the text is also converted to lowercase for vocabulary analysis.

Methods¶

Frames¶

For the scope of this project, eight frames were created to analyze their presence across the sample. Economic opportunity and technological advancement that this data center project could bring to Mongolia fall into the broader dimension of developmental benefits, while data sovereignty and governance frames show the national and institutional interests. Resource constraints about the topic will be represented by the energy and water constraint frames, and lastly, opposing environmental claims, both the environmental benefit and risk frames, were chosen because these are currently the main concerns about the project from the public.

Baseline Approach¶

The baseline approach consists of close reading of the articles across the sample and manually assigning frames. Each article was reviewed and assigned a binary label for each frame: 1 if present, 0 if absent. It should be noted that multiple frames could be assigned to the same article.

Baseline Dictionary Approach¶

Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF representations were applied to the clean text, which had been stripped of irrelevant content, normalized to lowercase, and assigned unique codes to each letter through Unicode, and operated to find the top terms appearing across the sample. During both representations, a dictionary of Mongolian stopwords was also applied to find more meaningful words in the interpretation.

For the Bag-of-Words method, the top 20 unigrams that appeared most frequently in the articles were found, while the TF-IDF method found the most distinctive 20 unigrams and bigrams across the articles.

Figure 1. Top terms found from BoW and TF-IDF representations across the sample.

These top 40 words, some of which overlapped, were then utilized to construct a dictionary of related terms and their associated frames. It should be noted that the terms in the dictionary weren’t actually in the top terms list; instead, they were constructed after being inspired by individual stems or components of the phrases appeared among the top results. For example, “хөрөнгө” and “оруулалт” were combined into “хөрөнгө оруулалт” (investment), and the term was assigned under the economic opportunity frame.

The dictionary was then run across each article to check for matching terms. If at least one pattern that was associated with a frame was found, the article containing that pattern will be assigned the frame.

Binary Bag-of-Words and Logistic Regression¶

TF-IDF and Logistic Regression¶

In these classification models, the text representations by the Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF were used. BoW used unigrams; TF-IDF used both unigrams and bigrams, and both representations had their stopwords removed. These representations subsequently acted as the input features of the model. Additionally, human-coded frame assignments from the baseline method were the target variable.

Then, logistic regression classifier was applied per frame to learn which word patterns increase or decrease the estimated probability of a frame being present.

For Bag-of-Words, logistic regression learned a coefficient for each word: a positive coefficient increased the predicted probability of a frame when the word was present, while a negative coefficient decreased it, holding other features constant.

For TF-IDF, words and two-word phrases were represented by weighted scores and their influence depended on both their TF-IDF scores and their learned coefficients: a higher score increased the predicted probability when the coefficient was positive and decreased it when the coefficient was negative, holding other features constant.

Since the sample these methods would train on was small, five-fold cross-validation was applied to test the model’s performance. Each model trained on 40 articles and predicted the remaining 10 per round. Vocabulary and TF-IDF weights were learned within each training fold.

Results¶

The human-coded results indicate that coverage primarily presented the initiative as an opportunity for technological and economic development. Technological advancement appeared in 94% of the articles, followed by economic opportunity in 86%. Environmental benefit and governance each appeared in around 40 articles (80%). Data sovereignty and energy constraints received less attention, appearing in 22 and 19 articles, respectively. Environmental risk and water constraints each appeared in only three articles. This distribution suggests that anticipated benefits and policy arrangements received substantially more attention than potential environmental costs and resource pressures.

Figure 2. The distribution of eight frames across the sample using the baseline method.

Opportunity-oriented framing was widespread across all three source types. All government-source articles contained economic opportunity, technology, and governance frames. Publicly funded sources consistently included technology and environmental benefit frames (100% each). Independent sources also frequently discussed technology (90%), economic opportunity (85%), environmental benefit (80%), and governance (80%). Thus, the emphasis on benefits extended beyond official government communication.

The clearest differences concerned sovereignty and constraints. Data sovereignty appeared in approximately 52% of independent-source articles, compared with 20% of publicly funded articles and none of the government-source articles. Environmental risk and water constraints appeared exclusively among independent sources, although each occurred in only about 8% of that group’s articles. Energy constraints received attention across all source types: 50% of government articles, 20% of publicly funded articles, and approximately 42% of independent articles. Independent sources therefore included a broader range of concerns, but their coverage remained predominantly focused on opportunities.

These differences should be interpreted descriptively. The government and publicly funded groups contained only four and five articles, respectively, so a single article changes their percentages considerably. Shared reporting across outlets may also contribute to similarities. The findings do not establish deliberate institutional framing strategies or imply that rarely discussed risks are unimportant.

Figure 3. Human-coded frame assignments across the articles by their source type

Evaluation¶

For baseline dictionary and Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF based logistic regression models, their precision, recall, and F1 scores were evaluated because classification errors may lead to unreliable conclusions about the presence of frames in news.

Binary BoW with logistic regression achieved the highest F1 for economic opportunity (0.94), data sovereignty (0.85), energy constraint (0.91), and governance (0.95). All three approaches achieved 0.94 for technology. The dictionary performed best for environmental benefit (0.93) and detected some environmental risk and water constraint cases, achieving F1 scores of 0.29 and 0.67, respectively. Both learned models scored zero for these rare frames. The performance from three methods depended substantially on the frame, with the rare frames remaining difficult to detect.

However, it should be noted that dictionary scores reflect agreement on the sample that was used to develop its rules, whereas learned-model scores reflect out-of-fold predictions.

Figure 4. Frame classification F1 performance through different approaches.

Error Analysis¶

Error analysis was conducted on the binary Bag-of-Words with logistic regression model because it had a better performance than TF-IDF with logistic regression.

Comparing its out-of-fold predictions with human-coded labels revealed an overprediction of common frames and missed occurrences of less frequent frames. Environmental benefit produced the most errors, comprising nine false positives and one false negative. Technology and governance generated six and four false positives, respectively, suggesting that shared vocabulary may have triggered frame assignments without sufficient contextual evidence. Economic opportunity produced four false positives and one false negative. On the other hand, data sovereignty generated five false negatives and one false positive, while energy constraints produced three false negatives. The model also missed all three positive articles for both environmental risk and water constraints.

Figure 5. Errors gotten from binary BoW + Logistic Regression model by frame

Based on the insights gotten from the error analysis, the model was repeated with balanced class weights (retaining the same features and five-fold splits) to address classification performance, particularly for rare frames. However, when comparing the original and revised models using the same five-fold splits, the revised model had more errors with the technology, data sovereignty, environmental benefit, and governance frames while bringing no change to the others. From these results, it could be deduced that weighting alone was insufficient to address the model’s errors.

Figure 5. Errors made by the revised model with balanced class weights, compared to the original.

Interpretation and Substantive Takeaways¶

Across the sample, economic opportunity, technology, environmental benefit, and governance frames were relatively dominant. Data sovereignty and energy constraints appeared less frequently; environmental risk and water constraints were rare. Overall, articles emphasized anticipated opportunities more than potential costs and resource pressures.

As for the outlet source types, government and publicly funded news sources predominantly emphasized opportunities, while independent sources included a broader range of frames. Environmental risk and water constraints appeared exclusively among independent sources, although they remained uncommon. These differences should be interpreted as descriptive because of the small and unequal numbers of articles in each news source group.

As for the model performances, BoW with logistic regression achieved higher F1 for economic opportunity, data sovereignty, energy constraints, and governance. The dictionary performed better for environmental benefit and the two rare frames.

All three approaches achieved the same F1 for technological advancement. However, dictionary results reflect development-sample agreement; learned-model results reflect cross-validation performance. The exploratory sensitivity check showed that balanced class weights did not improve performance by producing additional errors.

These findings describe how the project was represented across the sample. The results shouldn't be interpreted as evidence that dominant opportunity frames indicate that promised benefits will be delivered or the risks that were rare are negligible. The results also do not establish public opinion or reliable classification performance across broader Mongolian media.

Limitations and Future Work¶

This project concerns several limitations. First, the sample was small and imbalanced, containing only 50 articles and frames such as environmental risk and water constraint appearing in only three articles, making reliable evaluation challenging.

Second, similar or republished text across outlets had some presence even after the preprocessing stage of removing exact duplicates. This may have inflated cross-validation scores of the models if the similar text appeared in both training and evaluation folds.

Third, the methods employed had limited contextual understanding. BoW, TF-IDF, and pattern matching could have missed negation, context, and distinctions between general COP17 discussion and data center framing.

With more time, future work should expand the sample across more outlets, ideally including more articles discussing environmental risks and resource constraints because additional examples for learning and evaluating rare frames will be provided through them.

Also, near-duplicate articles should be identified and grouped within the same cross-validation fold to reduce overlap between training and evaluation texts. For the human-coded frame assignment, a second coder should review the articles and assign the 8 frames if they appear in the text to assess intercoder agreement and identify ambiguities in the frame definitions. Finally, evaluating the baseline dictionary and learned models on a separate, previously unseen sample would provide stronger evidence on the performance of these methods.
